newsitem.title: USA: The Hartford spins off 20 percent of life company.
newsitem.headline: The Hartford spins off 20 percent of life company.

text.p: Diversified insurer The Hartford said Monday it will spin off up to 20 percent of its life insurance operation as a publically traded company.
The initial public offering of stock in the new company is expected during the second quarter, the company said in a statement.
Industry analysts said the spinoff could raise up to $800 million for the company, and said its stock could trade as high as $40 per share.
The Hartford's share price jumped $3.125 to $78.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"The offering will enhance the group's shareholder value by recognising the market value of our life operations and strengthening The Hartford's financial position," said Ramani Ayer, chairman. "This strengthened financial position will provide The Hartford with improved flexibility to fund future growth."
Analysts hailed the move as a long-overdue recognition of the company's "crown jewel."
They said the IPO will likely be a hit with investors because The Hartford's life business has been growing well above the industry average.
This is thanks in large part to the company's huge variable annuities business, said analysts, who had speculated for months that a spinoff was in the works.
"Life is the crown jewel of The Hartford's operations," wrote Peter Wade of in a research report.

"It's the annuity business that makes it attractive. They added $12 billion in variable annuities which are low-risk, low-margin, but high ROE businesses, which are high-growth. It's sort of like mutual funds, with a tax-deferred wrapper."
An annuity is a contract that provides a periodic income at regular intervals for a specific time period. It is often used to fund retirement.
With variable annuities, the amount may fluctuate in relation to securities market values or other factors.
The Hartford's total life revenues grew by 17 percent in 1996 to $4.4 billion. Life core earnings were up by 14 percent to $251 million.
Its individual annuity revenues including deposits rose to $10.9 billion in 1996 against $7.6 billion in 1995.
"Hartford Life has been one of the most rapidly growing life insurance companies in the industry," said Mike Albanese, vice president at A.M. Best Co.

"They're raising capital in the lowest-cost means available, and they are also highlighting how undervalued their subsidiaries are," added Lehman Brothers' Wade. "They have a company embedded within them that has a 15-plus percentage growth rate, and probably almost a 20 percent return on equity, that prior to the announcement of this deal was trading at a discount to most property-casualty companies."
